title: Impact of polyphenol-rich olive mil waste water on the quality of life of patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma of the bladder
summary:
Background
Bladder cancer is a common malignancy that is difficult to treat in advanced stages. Standard therapy (surgery and chemotherapy) can cause significant side effects and often only modestly improves survival. Therefore, many patients seek complementary treatment options, such as plant-based compounds.
There is growing interest in so-called polyphenols—natural plant substances found, among other sources, in olives. They have antioxidant properties (protecting cells from harmful substances) and may help reduce inflammation as well as psychological distress such as anxiety and depression. Initial studies suggest that these compounds could improve the quality of life of cancer patients; however, robust evidence is still limited.

Research Question / Objective
This study investigates whether the intake of a polyphenol-rich olive extract can improve psychological well-being and quality of life in patients with bladder cancer.
The key question is:
Can short-term intake during hospitalization lead to measurable positive effects on mood, anxiety, and overall well-being?

Methods
A clinical study is planned involving bladder cancer patients who will consume olive water following surgical removal of the bladder.
The supplement is administered orally (as a drink).
The focus is on the early phase of hospital treatment, when psychological stress is particularly high.
Effects are assessed using questionnaires measuring quality of life and psychological status (e.g., anxiety, depression, overall well-being).
The study examines whether intake leads to rapid changes in psychological condition.

interventions.name: Arm 1: olive mill waste water, 2x one ampoule per day orally for 12 days

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All patients who will undergo radical cystectomy with ileal conduit diversion.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients who do not wish to participate in the study.
Patients incapable of giving consent.
Patients who cannot undergo surgery.
Patients under 21 years of age.
Pre-existing olive or grape allergy or intolerance.
Pregnant or breastfeeding patients.
Patients with a diagnosed phobia or depression.
